# Comparison of Investigator-Reported vs Centrally Adjudicated Major Adverse Cardiac Events

**Authors:** Prakriti Gaba; Deepak L. Bhatt; Gilles R. Dagenais; Jackie Bosch; Aldo P. Maggioni; Petr Widimsky; Darryl Leong; Keith A. A. Fox; Salim Yusuf; John W. Eikelboom

**Affiliations:** 1Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 2Population Health Research Institute, McMaster University and Hamilton Health Sciences, Hamilton, Canada | 3Division of Cardiology, Centro Studi ANMCO, Florence, Italy | 4Cardiocenter, University Hospital “Kralovske Vinohrady,” Prague, Czech Republic | 5University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom

## Abstract

Is there a difference between centrally adjudicated and investigator-reported cardiac events in the Cardiovascular Outcomes for People Using Anticoagulation Strategies (COMPASS) trial?

In this secondary analysis of the COMPASS randomized clinical trial, there were 10% to 15% fewer events as reported by adjudication vs investigator reporting for most end points. However, ischemic end points were highly concordant among most adjudicated and investigator-reported events.

These findings suggest that using investigator reporting for events in blinded randomized clinical trials may be a more efficient alternative to adjudication for the reporting of specific cardiac outcomes.

## Abstract

This secondary analysis of the Cardiovascular Outcomes for People Using Anticoagulation Strategies (COMPASS) randomized clinical trial compares investigator-reported vs central adjudicated cardiac events in patients with atherosclerotic vascular disease treated with rivaroxaban vs aspirin.

## Abstract

In the Cardiovascular Outcomes for People Using Anticoagulation Strategies (COMPASS) trial, there was a significant reduction in the adjudicated primary outcome among patients with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease randomized to dual pathway inhibition (rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily) vs aspirin monotherapy, but not with rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily vs aspirin monotherapy. Whether the results are similar without adjudication is unknown.

To examine the impact of dual pathway inhibition (with rivaroxaban plus aspirin) or rivaroxaban monotherapy compared with aspirin monotherapy on investigator-reported CV events and to understand the extent of concordance between investigator-reported and centrally adjudicated clinical events.

This is a secondary analysis of the COMPASS trial, an international, double-blind, double-dummy, randomized clinical trial with a 3-by-2 partial factorial design that evaluated participants with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease receiving rivaroxaban plus aspirin, rivaroxaban monotherapy, or aspirin monotherapy. End points were collected by blinded site investigators and adjudicated by a blinded clinical end point committee. Data were analyzed from March 2013 through February 2017.

Participants received dual inhibition pathway (2.5 mg rivaroxaban twice daily plus 100 mg aspirin once daily), rivaroxaban monotherapy (5 mg twice daily), or aspirin monotherapy (100 mg once daily).

The primary efficacy outcome was a composite of cardiovascular (CV) death, stroke, or myocardial infarction (MI). Adjudicated and investigator-reported end points were compared.

A total of 27 395 patients (mean [SD] age, 68.2 [7.9] years; 78.0% men) were assessed, including 9152 patients randomized to dual pathway inhibition, 9117 patients randomized to rivaroxaban monotherapy, and 9126 patients randomized to aspirin monotherapy. Adjudication reduced the number of events by 10% to 15% for most end points. Among investigator-reported end points, dual pathway inhibition significantly reduced the rate of the primary efficacy outcome compared with aspirin alone (411 patients [4.5%] vs 542 patients [5.9%]; hazard ratio [HR], 0.75 [95% CI, 0.66-0.85]; P < .001), with similar reduction in adjudicated end points, (379 patients [4.1%] vs 496 patients [5.4%]; HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.66-0.86]; P < .001). Likewise, effects on ischemic end points were highly concordant (κ statistic = 0.94 [95% CI, 0.93-0.95] for the primary composite end point). Unlike with adjudicated outcomes, there was a significant reduction in the primary end point with rivaroxaban monotherapy vs aspirin monotherapy using investigator-reported events (477 patients [5.2%] vs 542 patients [5.9%]; HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.78-0.99]; P = .04) compared with adjudicated events (448 patients [4.9%] vs 496 patients [5.4%]; HR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.79-1.03]; P = .12).

This secondary analysis of the COMPASS trial found that whether assessed by blinded site investigators or adjudicators, dual pathway inhibition significantly reduced CV events among patients with stable atherosclerotic disease compared with aspirin plus placebo. These findings suggest that using investigator-reported events in blinded clinical trials may be a more efficient alternative to adjudication.

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01776424

## Introduction

The purpose of central adjudication in clinical trials is to create high-quality data while maintaining low variability in outcomes and safety.1,2 Moreover, adjudication may be an important factor in reducing biases associated with intervention treatment groups, especially in unblinded trials. However, not all aspects of adjudication are favorable. Adjudication is expensive and time-consuming, and in the current climate of clinical trials, it is uncertain whether any improvement in precision in ascertaining end point events is eroded by investigator reporting as opposed to adjudication.3,4,5,6

The Cardiovascular Outcomes for People Using Anticoagulation Strategies (COMPASS) trial showed significant reductions in adjudicated events with rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily compared with aspirin monotherapy, but not with rivaroxaban monotherapy compared with aspirin monotherapy.7,8,9 Whether the cardiovascular (CV) benefits of rivaroxaban plus aspirin observed in the COMPASS trial are dependent on the central adjudication process is unknown. The aim of this secondary analysis of the COMPASS trial was to examine the impact of dual pathway inhibition (with rivaroxaban plus aspirin) or rivaroxaban monotherapy compared with aspirin monotherapy on investigator-reported CV events and to understand the extent of concordance between investigator-reported and centrally adjudicated clinical events.

## Methods

The COMPASS randomized clinical trial was approved by ethics committees at each participating site. All participants provided written informed consent as part of the trial process (Trial Protocol in Supplement 1). This study is reported following the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) reporting guideline.

### Study Design

The COMPASS trial was an international, double-blind, double-dummy, randomized clinical trial with a 3-by-2 partial factorial design that evaluated 27 395 participants with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease to receive either rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) plus aspirin (100 mg once daily) (dual inhibition pathway), rivaroxaban alone (5 mg twice daily), or aspirin alone (100 mg once daily).10 Prespecified end points were collected and reported by blinded site investigators. Case report forms were designed to help investigators apply outcome event definitions more precisely, and investigators were encouraged to send in event forms even if they were not certain it was an event. These events subsequently underwent evaluation using a computer algorithm. Events that were not confirmed were reviewed by the blinded event adjudication committee, comprising members of the trial steering committee according to a prespecified charter (Trial Protocol in Supplement 1 and eAppendix in Supplement 2). If there remained any uncertainty regarding a particular event, it was referred to the event adjudication chairs for a final decision. The chairs were also blinded but had access to the entire participant record when reviewing an event and could request additional information if required.

A flow diagram of the adjudication process is outlined in eFigure 1 in Supplement 2. Of note, the study was halted for superiority of the rivaroxaban plus aspirin group after a mean follow-up of 23 months. The criteria for stopping the trial early required analysis of the data at 2 scheduled interim meetings. If the observed hazard ratio (HR) for the primary efficacy outcome had crossed a prespecified critical value obtained using the corresponding modified Haybittle-Peto boundary, then the decision was made to terminate the trial.

### Clinical End Points

The primary efficacy outcome was a composite of CV death, stroke, or myocardial infarction (MI). The 3 secondary efficacy outcomes were composite ischemic stroke, MI, acute limb ischemia, or death from coronary heart disease; composite CV death, MI, ischemic stroke, or acute limb ischemia; and death from any cause. Other end points included the individual components of the primary and secondary efficacy outcomes, as well as the occurrence of angina, heart failure, and venous thromboembolism. Details regarding the collected end points have been previously published in the American College of Cardiology Foundation and American Heart Association Standardized Definitions for End Point Events in Cardiovascular Trials.10,11

### Statistical Analysis

In this analysis, investigator-reported end point events were compared with adjudicated end point events of patients in the dual inhibition pathway arm and rivaroxaban group vs those in the aspirin monotherapy group. No specific patient groups were excluded in this subanalysis. All analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. Univariate comparisons were performed using the χ2 or Fisher exact test for categorical variables, while the t test was used for continuous variables. Time-to-event outcomes were estimated by Kaplan-Meier rates and compared using the log-rank test. Comparisons in clinical outcomes among the rivaroxaban plus aspirin, rivaroxaban alone, and aspirin alone groups were assessed using hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs with a Cox proportional hazards model. Concordance was evaluated by the Cohen method and reported as a simple κ statistic with 95% CI. All tests were 2-sided, and P < .05 was considered statistically significant for all end points. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS statistical software version 9.4 (SAS Institute). Data were analyzed from March 2013 through February 2017.

## Results

### Study Population and Baseline Characteristics

The baseline characteristics of participants enrolled in the COMPASS trial have been previously published.12 In brief, a total of 27 395 patients (mean [SD] age, 68.2 [7.9] years; 78.0% men) were assessed, including 9152 patients randomized to dual pathway inhibition, 9117 patients randomized to rivaroxaban monotherapy, and 9126 patients randomized to aspirin monotherapy. All patients had a history of coronary artery disease (90.6%), peripheral artery disease (27.3%), or a combination of both. Median (range) time to follow-up was 23 (<1-47) months.

### Investigator-Reported Clinical Outcomes for Dual Pathway Inhibition vs Aspirin Monotherapy

The primary efficacy outcome reported by site investigators was significantly lower with dual pathway inhibition compared with aspirin monotherapy (411 patients [4.5%] vs 542 patients [5.9%]; HR, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.66-0.85]; P < .001). The event curves based on a Kaplan-Meier analysis of the primary efficacy end point are provided in the Figure, panel A. Rates of the 3 secondary efficacy outcomes, including a composite of ischemic stroke, MI, acute limb ischemia, or death from coronary heart disease; a composite of CV death, MI, ischemic stroke, or acute limb ischemia; and death from any cause, were also significantly lower with a dual pathway inhibition strategy compared with aspirin monotherapy (Table 1). When segregated by prespecified patient subgroups, these findings remained consistent (eFigure 2 in Supplement 2). Of note, the number of cardiovascular deaths was slightly increased in the adjudicated category, primarily due to a reclassification of a few non-CV deaths to CV deaths. The total number of deaths did not change (Table 1).

Patients treated with rivaroxaban monotherapy experienced significantly lower composite cardiovascular death, stroke, or myocardial infarction compared with those treated with aspirin monotherapy by investigator-reported but not CEC-adjudicated outcomes (B). HR indicates hazard ratio.*

### Investigator-Reported Clinical Outcomes for Rivaroxaban Monotherapy vs Aspirin Monotherapy

The primary efficacy outcome reported by site investigators was significantly lower with rivaroxaban compared with aspirin monotherapy (477 patients [5.2%] vs 542 patients [5.9%]; HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.78-0.99]; P = .04). The event curves based on a Kaplan-Meier analysis of the primary efficacy outcome are provided in the Figure, panel B. When segregated by prespecified patient subgroups, these findings remained consistent (eFigure 3 in Supplement 2). Secondary efficacy outcomes reported by site investigators were similarly lower with rivaroxaban compared with aspirin monotherapy (Table 2). Among individual end points, heart failure was higher among patients who received rivaroxaban monotherapy, although the differences did not reach statistical significance. Similar to the dual pathway inhibition analysis, the number of CV deaths was slightly increased in the adjudicated category in this analysis as well, primarily due to a reclassification of a few non-CV deaths to CV deaths. The total number of deaths did not change (Table 2).

### Investigator-Reported vs Centrally Adjudicated Clinical Outcomes

Among patients treated with dual pathway inhibition vs aspirin monotherapy, there were more primary efficacy outcome events reported by investigators than confirmed by the adjudicators; however, the difference between the dual pathway inhibition vs aspirin monotherapy groups remained similar for investigator-reported vs adjudicator-confirmed events. The centrally adjudicated primary efficacy outcome was noted in only 379 patients (4.1%) in the dual pathway inhibition group and 496 patients (5.4%) in the aspirin monotherapy group (HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.66-0.86]) (Table 1). This represents 32 fewer events in the dual pathway inhibition treatment group and 46 fewer events in the aspirin monotherapy group, a relative difference similar to that seen with an analysis of the postadjudication data. Analogous relationships were noted among all clinical end points, including major and minor bleeding (Table 1 and Table 2) and across geographic distributions (eTable 1 in Supplement 2). Although rates of stroke, acute limb ischemia, and venous thromboembolism were numerically higher when reported by site investigators compared with adjudicators, HRs of investigator-reported vs adjudicated end points remained similar (Table 1; eTable 2 in Supplement 2). Additional events reported by adjudicators were negligible.

Among patients treated with rivaroxaban monotherapy vs aspirin monotherapy, investigator reported rates of the primary efficacy outcome were numerically higher compared with adjudicated results. Importantly, the difference between the rivaroxaban and aspirin monotherapy groups was statistically significant using investigator-reported primary efficacy outcome events but not using the centrally adjudicated outcome events. In the adjudicated analysis, the primary efficacy outcome occurred in 448 patients (4.9%) in the rivaroxaban monotherapy group and 496 patients (5.4%) in the aspirin monotherapy group (HR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.79-1.03]) (Table 2). This represents a decrease in the number of events by 29 in the rivaroxaban monotherapy arm and 48 in the aspirin monotherapy arm.

Rates of concordance between investigator-reported and adjudicated events were high across a variety of ischemic end points in the dual pathway inhibition and aspirin monotherapy treatment groups. Site investigators and adjudicators agreed on the presence of the primary efficacy outcome in 372 patients who underwent treatment with dual pathway inhibition and 493 patients who received aspirin monotherapy. The CEC identified only 7 additional events among patients treated with dual pathway inhibition and 3 events among patients treated with aspirin monotherapy not reported by site investigators. Overall, the agreement between these groups for the primary efficacy outcome was strong (κ = 0.94 [95% CI, 0.93-0.95]). Other individually evaluated ischemic end points revealed similarly strong concordance trends, even across the rivaroxaban monotherapy and aspirin monotherapy treatment groups (Table 3 and Table 4). An exception to these concordant results was acute limb ischemia.

## Discussion

In this secondary analysis of the COMPASS randomized clinical trial, we found that among participants with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease who were randomized to receive rivaroxaban plus aspirin (dual inhibition pathway), rivaroxaban monotherapy, or aspirin monotherapy, central adjudication reduced the number of investigator-reported events by 10% to 15% for most end points. Estimates of treatment effects and concordance remained remarkably similar between investigator reported and adjudicated events. In keeping with the original trial results, the risk of the investigator-reported primary efficacy outcome of CV death, MI, or stroke was significantly lower in patients who received dual pathway inhibition compared with those who received aspirin monotherapy.13 Rates of secondary and other individual end points were also lower in patients treated with dual pathway inhibition compared with those treated with aspirin monotherapy.

These findings support the results of several recent studies that have demonstrated strong similarities between investigator-reported and adjudicated events in blinded randomized clinical trials. In the Reduction of Cardiovascular Events with Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial (REDUCE-IT), for instance, both the investigator-reported and adjudicated composite outcome of CV death, MI, stroke, coronary revascularization, and unstable angina requiring hospitalization showed similar and statistically significant results among patients treated with icosapent ethyl vs placebo.3 Although rates of individual end points slightly differed, the overall treatment effect remained the same. Similarly, an analysis of the Stabilization of Atherosclerotic Plaque by Initiation of Darapladib Therapy (STABILITY) trial revealed no important differences between investigator-reported vs adjudicated events, including death or nonfatal MI, but did demonstrate high concordance (>80%).4 As with ischemic end points, heart failure–related end points in blinded trials have also shown high concordance between site investigator–reported events vs centrally adjudicated events, as was recently seen in both the Sotagliflozin in Patients with Diabetes and Recent Worsening Heart Failure (SOLOIST-WHF)14 and Sotagliflozin in Patient with Diabetes and Chronic Kidney Disease (SCORED) trials.15

Contrary to previous beliefs, there are several advantages to considering investigator-reported events in blinded randomized clinical trials. First, investigator reporting is substantially less expensive and more efficient than central adjudication.16,17 Second, in clinical trials where there is treatment masking at various levels (eg, double-blinded clinical trials where participants and investigators are blinded to treatment assignment), investigator-reported events may allow for isolation of the effect of a treatment intervention itself without the introduction of substantial bias. Moreover, investigator reporting reduces the complexity of trial conduct, mitigating the need for a designated CEC that oversees and confirms all end points.

Consistent findings have been noted in the broader literature and have even changed clinical guidelines. The recent Prospective Comparison of ARNI with ARB Global Outcomes in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (PARAGON-HF) trial18 is one example. Although the trial did not generate enough events to meet significance for its prespecified adjudicated composite end point of heart failure hospitalization or CV death, incorporation of investigator-reported events led to statistically significant lower heart failure hospitalization or CV death among patients treated with sacubitril or valsartan. On detailed retrospective review, Felker et al18 found that many of the 566 primary end point events originally discounted by the CEC represented true heart failure events and were missed due to stringent adjudication criteria enforced during the trial.18 In light of these findings, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded the indication of the medication to patients with eligible chronic heart failure with ejection fraction greater than 40%. Retrospective analyses of the recent Prospective ARNI versus ACE Inhibitor Trial to Determine Superiority in Reducing Heart Failure Events after MI (PARADISE-MI) trial19,20 as well as other older trials, including the CHARM-PRESERVED and PURSUIT trials,21 in which there was improved power and sample size in the investigator-reported arm, have revealed analogous outcomes.1,22

Nonetheless, there are circumstances in which increasing capture of end point events with investigator reporting may not increase study power. Rather, it may dilute the signal-to-noise ratio. Further studies exploring in which circumstances investigator reporting will enhance a true clinical signal are needed.

Taken together, these results beg the question of whether adjudication should be required routinely for all placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trials, especially those in which there is investigator blinding.23,24 Using investigator-reported events in blinded clinical trials may be a more efficient alternative to adjudication. In some cases, adjudication may underestimate the effectiveness of a treatment or preclude the identification of an effective treatment altogether. Further studies are required to more systematically address these lingering questions.

### Limitations

There are a several potential limitations to consider. First, this is a single trial study, outlining the concordance between investigator-reported and centrally adjudicated events. Site investigators in this trial may have applied different criteria for certain end points due to site-specific practices in this multicenter trial. Moreover, training and support provided to site investigators, along with the experience of site investigators with event reporting and classification, may have varied across sites, influencing the way in which events were ultimately recorded by site investigators. Although case report forms were designed to help investigators apply outcome event definitions more precisely, the results of the present analysis may not be replicated in other studies with site investigators who are not trained as well on end point classification as they were in COMPASS. Rates of acute limb ischemia were not as strongly concordant as the other ischemic parameters and may have been the result of subjectivity in diagnosis or stringent adjudication criteria. Moreover, this was not a trial in which routine imaging was used, and expertise was needed to interpret the results (eg, expansion of a cerebral hematoma requiring radiology confirmation). Nor was it a trial in which investigators were asked to report every considered event to the project office without themselves assessing whether the events constituted an outcome event. One may speculate that in both the aforementioned instances, adjudication may be useful. Additionally, because the study was halted for superiority of the rivaroxaban plus aspirin group after a mean follow-up of 23 months, early termination may have impacted the number of overall outcomes reported. If the trial had been completed, perhaps the efficacy of rivaroxaban monotherapy vs aspirin monotherapy would have been evident even among adjudicated events.

## Conclusions

In this secondary analysis of the COMPASS randomized clinical trial, there was strong concordance between most investigator-reported and CEC-adjudicated events. Whether assessed by blinded site investigators or blinded adjudicators, treatment with dual pathway inhibition significantly reduced the occurrence of adverse CV events among participants with stable atherosclerotic disease compared with aspirin monotherapy. Using investigator-reported events in blinded clinical trials may be a less expensive (but equally valid and more sensitive) alternative to adjudication for the evaluation of CV outcomes. Future systematic analyses of additional large trials will help further clarify whether adjudication remains a necessary means by which to assess clinical outcomes in blinded randomized clinical trials.
